sentences.text: He read everything the library had, which was one book and a chapter in another, and then read online for six weeks, and this is what he found out.
She sends a sound and the sound comes back and the time it takes tells her how far.
That much everybody knows.
What almost nobody knows is how much comes back with it.
The pitch of the return tells her whether the thing is coming or going.
The shape of the return tells her the texture — a curtain and a plank at the same distance sound completely different, and the difference is not subtle to her.
Overlapping returns give her a moth's wingbeat frequency, which is how she can tell one insect from another in flight, in the dark, at four metres, in about the time it takes a person to blink.
She does not build a fuzzy sense of the room.
She builds a room.
The bit that took him longest to accept was the resolution.

He assumed, because everybody assumes it, that sound must be a coarse instrument — that she would be getting an approximate lumpy version of the world compared to the crisp one a person gets from eyes.
That is not what the numbers say.
At close range a bat can resolve a difference of well under a millimetre in the distance to a surface.
She can find a wire in the dark that a person cannot see in daylight.
There is no sense in which she is getting a rough draft.
Joaquim sat with that for about a week and then got hold of the thing that mattered, and he got hold of it in the attic at nine at night with his back against a trunk.
That bat has never seen the room.
Not once.
That attic has not had a working bulb since the 1990s and she is nocturnal and she has spent her entire life in and around a black space under a roof.
There is no version of that room in her head made of light.
There has never been one and there is not going to be one.
And she knows it completely.
Better than he does.

She knows where every beam is and every nail and the loose board by the water tank and the exact position of the trunk he sits against, and she has never once bumped into any of it, and she is not managing or coping or compensating.
She is not doing a worse version of seeing.
She is doing a whole thing, all the way, that arrives at a room.

He wrote that sentence in the back of an exercise book and looked at it for a while and then wrote underneath it, in smaller letters, the thing he had actually been trying to get at: *Nobody feels sorry for a bat.* Nobody stands in a doorway watching a bat's hands.
Nobody moves a chest on a landing for a bat.
Every book he had read described what she does with something close to awe, and not one of them had ever once described it as a way of getting by.
